In [[econometrics]], the '''method of simulated moments (MSM)''' (also called '''simulated method of moments'''<ref name="NBERw13115">{{cite journal |doi=10.3386/w13115 |title=Implications of Search Frictions: Matching Aggregate and Establishment-level Observations |last=Cooper |first=Russell |author-link2=John Haltiwanger |first2=John |last2=Haltiwanger |last3=Willis |first3=Jonathan L. |journal=NBER Working Paper No. 13115 |date=May 2007 |doi-access=free }}</ref>) is a [[structural estimation]] technique introduced by [[Daniel McFadden]].<ref>{{cite journal |first=D. |last=McFadden |year=1989 |jstor=1913621 |title=A Method of Simulated Moments for Estimation of Discrete Response Models Without Numerical Integration |journal=[[Econometrica]] |volume=57 |issue=5 |pages=995–1026 |doi=10.2307/1913621 |url=http://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/1721.1/63887/1/methodofsimulate00mcfa.pdf |hdl=1721.1/63887 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> It extends the [[generalized method of moments]] to cases where theoretical [[moment function]]s cannot be evaluated directly, such as when moment functions involve high-dimensional [[integral]]s.  MSM's earliest and principal applications have been to research in [[industrial organization]], after its development by [[Ariel Pakes]], David Pollard, and others, though applications in [[consumption (economics)|consumption]] are emerging. Although the method requires the user to specify the distribution from which the simulations are to be drawn, this requirement can be 
relaxed through the use of an entropy maximizing distribution.<ref>{{cite journal |first=S. M. |last=Schennach |year=2014 |title=Entropic Latent Variable Integration via Simulation |journal=[[Econometrica]] |volume=82 |issue=1 |pages=345-385 | doi=10.3982/ECTA9748 | url=https://ideas.repec.org/a/wly/emetrp/v82y2014i1p345-385.html |hdl=10419/79553 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==GMM v.s. MSM==

*<math>\hat{\beta}_{GMM}=\operatorname{argmin}\,m(x,\beta)'Wm(x,\beta)</math>, 
where <math>m(x,\beta)</math> is the moment condition and W is a matrix. Using the optimal W matrix leads to efficient estimator.
*<math>\hat{\beta}_{MSM}=\operatorname{argmin}\,\hat{m}(x,\beta)'W\hat{m}(x,\beta)</math>, 
where <math>\hat{m}(x,\beta)</math> is the simulated moment condition and <math>E[\hat{m}(x,\beta)]=m(x,\beta)</math>

==MSM v.s. Indirect Inference==
MSM is a special case of [[Indirect Inference]]. While Indirect Inference allows the researcher to use any of the features of sample statistics as a basis for comparison of moments and data, the name MSM applies only when those statistics are moments of the data, i.e. averages, across the sample of functions defined for a single sample element.<ref>{{cite book |first=Anthony |last=Smith |title=New Palgrave Dictionary |chapter-url=http://www.econ.yale.edu/smith/palgrave7.pdf |chapter=Indirect Inference }}</ref>
